title: Excavate irrigation trenches in established landscapes

lessons.title: Planning and marking the trench
lessons.html:
Planning and marking the trench

In an established landscape, such as an existing garden, park, golf course or office park, there are already lawns, beds, trees, paving and services under the ground. Digging an irrigation trench here must be done with care so that the garden is not damaged and hidden pipes and cables are not hit.

Read the plan

  • The irrigation plan shows where pipes run, their size and depth.
  • Your supervisor will tell you the trench width and depth for each pipe.
  • Ask about anything that is not clear before you start digging.

Find services first

Under the ground there may be electrical cables, water pipes, sewer pipes, telephone and fibre cables, gas pipes and old irrigation lines. Hitting a power cable can kill you.

  • Look at site drawings of services and ask the client or site manager.
  • Look for signs: manhole covers, valve boxes, light poles, meter boxes, warning tape or markers.
  • A cable detector may be used by a trained person.
  • Where services are near, dig by hand with care. Never use a pick or trencher there.
  • If you uncover a cable or pipe that was not expected, stop and tell your supervisor.

Mark out the trench

  1. Use pegs and string, or marking paint, to show the line of the trench.
  2. Keep the line straight between points, and as shown on the plan.
  3. Route around tree trunks. Digging close to a tree cuts its roots and can kill it or make it fall. Follow your supervisor's instructions for working near trees; often the trench must go around the tree or the roots are tunnelled under by hand.

Protect the garden

  • Lay plastic sheets or tarps next to the trench to put soil on, so lawns and paving stay clean.
  • Lift plants in the path of the trench and keep them in the shade with roots covered and moist.
  • Tell the client which areas will be disturbed.

lessons.title: Digging the trench safely
lessons.html:
Digging the trench

Steps

  1. Cut and lift the sods along the marked line with a flat spade. Cut them in neat squares or strips of even thickness. Stack them grass side to grass side on the sheet in the shade, and keep them moist.
  2. Remove the topsoil and put it on its own heap.
  3. Dig the subsoil to the required depth and put it on a separate heap. Keeping topsoil and subsoil apart means the good soil can go back on top.
  4. Keep the sides straight and the bottom even, with no sharp stones that could damage the pipe.
  5. Check depth and width with a measuring stick as you go.
  6. Keep spoil heaps back from the edge of the trench so soil does not fall back in and the edges do not collapse.

Tools

  • Flat spade for sods, round-nose spade, pick (not near services), trenching shovel, wheelbarrow, measuring stick.
  • A mechanical trencher may be used in open areas by trained operators only.

Safety

  • Wear boots, gloves, a hat and eye protection when using a pick.
  • Keep a safe distance between workers using spades and picks.
  • Barricade open trenches with tape, cones or barriers, especially in public places. Cover trenches left open overnight.
  • Lift with your legs, not your back.
  • Drink water and rest in the shade in hot weather.
  • Never enter a deep trench that could collapse. Irrigation trenches are usually shallow, but if a trench is deep, it must be supported as your supervisor says.

Finishing

  • Remove stones and roots from the bottom.
  • Tell the supervisor the trench is ready for checking before the pipe is laid.
  • Keep the work area tidy at the end of every day.

Key points

  • Read the plan and find underground services before digging.
  • Dig by hand near services and stop if you find an unexpected cable or pipe.
  • Protect trees, lawns and paving.
  • Lift sods neatly and keep topsoil and subsoil in separate heaps.
  • Barricade open trenches and keep spoil back from the edge.
